claim: String pulling is one of the most extensively used approaches in comparative psychology to evaluate the understanding of causal relationships.
source: String pulling is one of the most extensively used approaches in comparative psychology to evaluate the understanding of causal relationships (Jacobs and Osvath, 2015), with most research focused on mammals and birds, where a food item is visible to the animal but accessible only by pulling on a string attached to the reward (Taylor et al., 2010; Range et al., 2012; Jacobs and Osvath, 2015; Wakonig et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Jacobs and Osvath, 2015; Taylor et al., 2010; Range et al., 2012; Wakonig et al., 2021) that establish string pulling as a standard method in comparative psychology.

claim: Most research on string pulling has focused on mammals and birds.
source: String pulling is one of the most extensively used approaches in comparative psychology to evaluate the understanding of causal relationships (Jacobs and Osvath, 2015), with most research focused on mammals and birds, where a food item is visible to the animal but accessible only by pulling on a string attached to the reward (Taylor et al., 2010; Range et al., 2012; Jacobs and Osvath, 2015; Wakonig et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to research on mammals and birds (Taylor et al., 2010; Range et al., 2012; Jacobs and Osvath, 2015; Wakonig et al., 2021).

claim: The complexity of the string-pulling paradigm can be altered by manipulating the number and mutual positions of the strings and reward.
source: The complexity of the string-pulling paradigm can be altered by manipulating the number and mutual positions of the strings and reward, allowing the investigation of different aspects of cognition (Jacobs and Osvath, 2015; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to research describing manipulation of string-pulling paradigms (Jacobs and Osvath, 2015; Wang et al., 2019).

claim: Multiple mechanisms can be involved in the string-pulling task, including the proximity principle, perceptual feedback and means-end understanding.
source: Multiple mechanisms can be involved in the string-pulling task, including the proximity principle, perceptual feedback and means-end understanding (Taylor et al., 2012; Wasserman et al., 2013; Jacobs and Osvath, 2015; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to research identifying these mechanisms (Taylor et al., 2012; Wasserman et al., 2013; Jacobs and Osvath, 2015; Wang et al., 2021).

claim: The principle of proximity refers to animals preferring to pull the reward that is closest to them.
source: The principle of proximity refers to animals preferring to pull the reward that is closest to them (Jacobs and Osvath, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation defining the proximity principle (Jacobs and Osvath, 2015).

claim: Taylor et al., 2012 proposed that the success of New Caledonian crows in string-pulling tasks is based on a perceptual-motor feedback loop.
source: Taylor et al., 2012 proposed that the success of New Caledonian crows in string-pulling tasks is based on a perceptual-motor feedback loop, where the reward gradually moves closer to the animal as they pull the strings.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Taylor et al., 2012 describing their proposal about New Caledonian crows.

claim: If the visual signal of the reward approaching is restricted, crows with no prior string-pulling experience are unable to solve the broken string task.
source: If the visual signal of the reward approaching is restricted, crows with no prior string-pulling experience are unable to solve the broken string task (Taylor et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Taylor et al., 2012 describing experimental results with crows.

claim: Means-end understanding is expressed as goal-directed behavior, which involves the deliberate and planned execution of a sequence of steps to achieve a goal.
source: Means-end understanding is expressed as goal-directed behavior, which involves the deliberate and planned execution of a sequence of steps to achieve a goal (Jacobs and Osvath, 2015; Torres Ortiz et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations defining means-end understanding (Jacobs and Osvath, 2015; Torres Ortiz et al., 2019).

claim: String-pulling studies have directly tested means-end comprehension in various species.
source: String-pulling studies have directly tested means-end comprehension in various species (Riemer et al., 2014; Jacobs and Osvath, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to research testing means-end comprehension (Riemer et al., 2014; Jacobs and Osvath, 2015).

claim: Most animals fail in string-pulling tasks when they have to spontaneously solve them.
source: Most animals fail in such string-pulling tasks when they have to spontaneously solve them, but they can be trained to recognize that an interrupted string is useless through trial-and-error learning (Mayer et al., 2014; Torres Ortiz et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to research showing animals' failure in spontaneous string-pulling tasks (Mayer et al., 2014; Torres Ortiz et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019).

claim: Animals can be trained to recognize that an interrupted string is useless through trial-and-error learning.
source: Most animals fail in such string-pulling tasks when they have to spontaneously solve them, but they can be trained to recognize that an interrupted string is useless through trial-and-error learning (Mayer et al., 2014; Torres Ortiz et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to research showing animals can learn through trial-and-error (Mayer et al., 2014; Torres Ortiz et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019).

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to research on bumblebee string-pulling (Alem et al., 2016; Wen et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024) and the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: The performance of bumblebees in string-pulling studies could be explained by associative learning.

claim: There is no spontaneous comprehension of the significance of the gap in bumblebees without string-pulling experience.
